summary:
Gibraltar is a self-governing territory with its own Parliament and its own Supreme Court, which between them make and interpret its civil and criminal law. Measures enacted by the United Kingdom do not apply here of their own force: the United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and the single-sex-services code issued in 2025 bind Gibraltar only if extended by Order in Council. No such extension appears in the sourced material.

No process exists in Gibraltar for changing a legal gender marker, and the sourced material records that transgender persons are not permitted to change legal gender. A trans visitor therefore travels on a document whose marker cannot be altered by any local route, and can expect to be read in public and at the border under that marker.

Protection against discrimination on grounds of gender reassignment, alongside sexual orientation, has been in place since 2007. Gibraltar's Parliament amended the hate-crime and hate-speech provisions of the Crimes Act 2011 by a bill passed in September 2013, in force from 10 October 2013, covering sexual orientation; in July 2026 Parliament passed a bill extending those hate-crime and hate-speech protections to transgender identity.

Also in July 2026, Parliament passed a bill making it an offence to offer or to practise conversion therapy. Same-sex marriage has been lawful since a bill passed unanimously in December 2016 amending the Civil Marriage Act, and civil partnerships have been available since 2014, so a visitor travelling with a same-sex partner can expect that relationship to be legally recognised.

The sourced material contains nothing on document checks, entry screening, bathroom or facility access, or healthcare access for trans visitors in Gibraltar, and no incidents of violence against transgender people are recorded in it.
tangentialFactors:
Gibraltar's trajectory on sexual-orientation and gender-status law is measured against expectations set for overseas territories by the United Kingdom House of Commons Foreign Affairs Committee, whose Seventh Report of 2007-08 set accountability and good-governance standards for territories such as Gibraltar, and whose 2008 inquiry recommended making discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender status illegal across all overseas territories.

Public opinion has not always tracked the legislature. A December 2015 consultation on amending the Civil Marriage Act left Gibraltarians polarised before the bill went to Parliament, with an inter-ministerial committee chaired by a government minister weighing all viewpoints and the main parties indicating support for the change.

Hostility has surfaced in ways the state has had to answer publicly. Following an incident of anti-gay abuse in July 2021, the Ministry for Justice and Equality said it would urgently consider legislation to tackle what it called disgusting lurking homophobia, and the Chief Minister, Fabian Picardo, used the same phrase about social-media abuse during Pride month.

The United Kingdom's own equality framework, which does apply in the United Kingdom, supplies the comparator a visitor may be tempted to assume: in Gibraltar it reaches only through a formal extension instrument, and the sourced material records no extension of the Equality Act 2010 or of the 2025 single-sex-services code.
localsOnly:
Residents have had equal legal standing on sexual orientation since 1993, with the age of consent equalised at 16 for all sexual activity: the Supreme Court of Gibraltar ruled on 8 April 2011 that the higher age of 18 for gay sex was unconstitutional, and the gender-neutral Crimes Act 2011, approved in August 2011, set the equal age of 16 with effect from 23 November 2012. Before that, gay male minors faced a discriminatory age of 18, and a private member's bill to equalise consent was defeated in Parliament on 18 May 2009.

On 10 April 2013 the Supreme Court held that section 5(2) of the Adoption Act 1951 violated the Gibraltar Constitution, de jure legalising LGBT adoption, after a long-term lesbian couple denied adoption for want of legal recognition of their relationship brought the challenge; the government amended the law through the 2014 civil-partnership legislation. The Adoption Act 2023 took full effect on 18 April 2024 and expressly allows same-sex couples to adopt without discrimination.

In February 2021 Gibraltar enacted a surrogacy law permitting non-commercial, altruistic surrogacy for married couples or civil partners unable to conceive, with automatic recognition of children of same-sex couples conceived through artificial insemination. In June 2017 the Gibraltar Health Authority approved an amendment to its in vitro fertilisation policy allowing lesbian couples to access assisted reproductive technology.

In July 2021 the Ministry for Justice and Equality began investigating a further proposal to make denigration of a person on the basis of sexual orientation a specific criminal offence, alongside the in-force 2013 hate-crime provision. The July 2026 measures extending hate-crime and hate-speech protection to transgender identity and creating a conversion-therapy offence are recorded as bills passed by Parliament; the sourced material does not state the date of royal assent or commencement for either.
